title: Copper damascene process-based high-performance thin-film lithium tantalate modulators

paper_content.abstract: The conversion between electrical and optical signals underpins modern optical communication systems and increasingly requires tight co-integration with electronics at short length scales. Thin-film lithium tantalate has emerged as a promising electro-optic platform due to its large Pockels coefficient, low bias drift, and high power handling, yet its integration with standardized microelectronic processes remains limited. Here we show that incorporating the copper Damascene process into thin-film lithium tantalate modulators enables a scalable, electronics-compatible fabrication approach. The resulting devices exhibit approximately 10% lower microwave loss than conventional gold-electrode designs, while simultaneously supporting watt-level on-chip optical power handling and maintaining a stable quasi-static half-wave voltage from 1 Hz to 1 MHz, with a bias point drift of only 0.4 dB over a 15-hour period when operated at 1.75 mW on-chip optical power. High-speed transmission experiments demonstrate line rates of 416 Gbit/s (PAM4) and 540 Gbit/s (PAM8) below the 25% soft-decision forward-error-correction threshold, together with watt-level on-chip optical power handling. These results establish a practical route toward scalable chip-on-wafer integration of electro-optic modulators with microelectronic circuits.
paper_content.introduction:
Integrated electro-optic (EO) modulators provide a scalable platform for converting information between electrical and optical domains, serving as key building blocks for high-capacity optical communications 1–3 and emerging chip-to-chip interconnects 4,5. Recent progress in thin-film lithium niobate and thin-film lithium tantalate photonics has transformed traditional bulk devices 6,7. The adoption of a layered “on-insulator” structure, combined with improved etching techniques, enables strong optical confinement and allows electrodes to be placed closer to the waveguide, thereby enhancing modulation efficiency. This structure also facilitates velocity matching between optical and microwave signals, resulting in higher modulation bandwidths. However, as the electrode gap is reduced to achieve tighter optical confinement and stronger modulation, the currents in the signal line and ground plane become increasingly concentrated near the gap due to the electromagnetic proximity effect 8. This enhanced current concentration increases the per-unit-length resistance of the transmission line, leading to higher microwave loss. The resulting loss limits further improvements in voltage–bandwidth performance. Employing electrodes with periodic microstructured “T-rails” mitigates the proximity effect by introducing a larger effective gap while preserving the electric-field distribution required for efficient modulation 9–12. An alternative approach to reducing microwave loss replaces conventional gold electrodes with low-resistivity metals, such as copper which has a resistivity approximately 24% lower than gold 13.

While continuous efforts have been made to extend the voltage–bandwidth performance of thin-film lithium niobate and lithium tantalate modulators 14,15, most reported devices remain standalone prototypes, requiring bulky electrical probes and external control electronics. Meanwhile, AI-based applications are driving an ever-growing demand for higher data throughput, lower latency, and improved energy efficiency in modern computing systems 16. To meet these requirements, co-packaged optics (CPO) has emerged as a transformative technology that tightly integrates photonics and electronics 17. Such integration reduces high-frequency signal degradation, reduces energy consumption, and enables large-scale system scalability. Among various integration approaches, three-dimensional (3D) integration, as illustrated in Figure 1(a), offers the shortest metal interconnects by vertically stacking photonic and electronic chips, thereby minimizing signal loss and improving overall efficiency 18. While this stacking is typically achieved through flip-chip bonding using microbumps 19, the industry is transitioning toward hybrid copper-copper bonding 20. In this approach, copper surfaces are directly joined through thermally activated diffusion, eliminating solder interfaces and thereby reducing parasitic effects. A key enabler of this transition is planarized copper metallization achieved via the copper Damascene process, already widely adopted in both microelectronics 21 and silicon photonics 22. However, ferroelectric photonic platforms still rely on conventional gold electrodes, highlighting the need for further innovation to achieve fully integrated, high-performance photonic–electronics systems.

Here, we address this challenge by incorporating the copper Damascene process into the fabrication of lithium tantalate photonic integrated circuits (PICs). This approach leverages a mature, low-cost, and widely adopted method used for metallization in microelectronics and silicon photonics. Using this process, we demonstrate integrated electro-optic modulators with microwave losses approximately 10% lower than those employing conventional gold electrodes, while preserving the intrinsic benefits of thin-film lithium tantalate, including low optical loss, high modulation efficiency, and broad modulation bandwidth. The resulting planar electrode surface also supports direct chip-on-chip and chip-on-wafer bonding with driver electronics.
paper_content.results:
Fabrication. The devices were fabricated from a commercially available X-cut thin-film lithium tantalate (TFLT) wafer (NANOLN), which consists of 600nm of lithium tantalate (LiTaO3, LT), 4.7µm of SiO2, and a 525µm-thick high-resistivity silicon substrate. The TFLT PICs were manufactured using an etching technique based on a diamond-like carbon hard mask, which can reliably produce both lithium niobate and lithium tantalate PICs 23,24. The etch depth of the LT was 320nm, leaving a 280nm-thick slab for efficient electro-optic modulation and proper phase matching between microwave and optical signals.

Next, the copper Damascene process, outlined in Figure 1(b), was introduced to fabricate traveling-wave electrodes. This Damascene process differs from silicon nitride Damascene methods 25, which reduce optical propagation losses in waveguides whereas we apply it to copper electrodes to minimize microwave loss. In this process, dielectric trenches are patterned and filled by electroplated copper followed by chemical–mechanical polishing (CMP). This process produces well-defined electrodes with a smooth surface potentially suitable for chip-on-wafer bonding. Further information on the fabrication is available in the Methods. Figure 1 (c) shows two fabricated Cu-TFLT MZMs extending over an effective modulation length of 6mm. Figure 1 (d) illustrates the fabricated 4-inch wafer with hundreds of Cu-TFLT MZMs, highlighting its potential for scalable integration of next-generation photonic systems. To improve the wafer’s uniformity following the CMP process, inactive regions feature a filler copper pattern, which is visible in Figure 1(c-e). As respectively shown in Figure 1(e-g), each modulator consists of 50:50 1×2 multimode interference (MMI) couplers, EO phase shifters operating in a push-pull configuration, and double-layer tapers for enhanced PIC-to-fiber coupling efficiency 26 (Figure S1). As illustrated in Figure 1(f), the tight confinement of the modulator’s microwave and optical modes ensures strong overlap between the two fields and thus enhanced modulation efficiency.

Electrical Transmission. To assess the potential of copper as an electrode material for high-performance modulators, we characterized the electrical properties of fabricated copper Damascene CPWs, including resistivity and microwave performance, and compared them with their conventional gold-based counterparts. Figure 2 (a) shows a photograph of the test structures. For context, Figure 2 (b) presents the bulk resistivity of the seven most conductive elemental metals commonly used in microelectronics and photonics. Although thin films are typically employed in these applications, their resistivity depends on thickness and fabrication process; thus, bulk values are used here for a general comparison. Silver (1.59µΩcm) exhibits the lowest resistivity, followed by copper (1.68µΩcm), which is only 5.6% higher, and gold (2.21µΩcm), which is 39% higher 27. We focus on copper and gold due to the impracticality of using silver (see Discussion).

Figure 2 (c) compares the measured resistivity of thin-film gold and copper and its evolution with time. The gold thin film (796nm) was deposited by electron beam evaporation, and the copper thin film (1170nm) by electroplating. Both were formed on silicon carrier wafers with a 2µm silicon dioxide layer and characterized using a four-point probing and mechanical profilometry. The electroplated copper exhibited a 24% decrease in resistivity within 48 hours at room temperature due to self-annealing 28, stabilizing at 2.04µΩcm - approximately 20% lower than that of gold. Studies suggest that the resistivity of electroplated copper could be further reduced to 1.77µΩcm 29 via process optimization. Using these measured values, we modeled the microwave behavior of the fabricated CPWs through full-wave electromagnetic simulations (Figure S2). Figure 2 (d) shows the simulated microwave loss of a 16mm-long copper Damascene CPW with a 6µm gap and a 27µm signal line, alongside simulated CPWs with varying resistivities but identical geometries. The measured microwave loss agrees well with the simulation, validating the model. The data indicate that copper electrodes yield approximately 10% lower microwave loss than gold, while the propagation index and characteristic impedance change by less than 0.3%. The dependence of the microwave effective index on design parameters is provided in Figure S3.

Electro-optic Modulation. A direct approach to assess the modulators’ performance is to measure their EO response, including the quasi-static half-wave voltage (Vπ) and the 3 dB EO bandwidth. Finite-element simulations (COMSOL Multiphysics) were performed to analyze the VπL product and optical loss for various modulator geometries. A design with 6µm electrode gap and a 4µm-wide waveguide was selected. This relatively wide waveguide maintains a similar VπL and optical loss while allowing a larger electrode gap that reduces microwave loss (Figure S4) 30. A 100µm-long adiabatic linear taper connects the modulation region to the single-mode routing waveguide, ensuring single-mode operation. The quasi-static Vπ was measured by applying a low-frequency triangular voltage signal to the CPW electrode and recording the optical output simultaneously. Figure 3 (a) shows the normalized transmission of a modulator as a function of the applied voltage, linearly swept at 100Hz, exhibiting a near-sinusoidal response with a Vπ of 1.7V. For a device length of 16mm, this corresponds to a VπL of 2.7V·cm, closely matching the simulated value of 2.64V·cm. The inset dB-scale plot shows an extinction ratio of 20dB, suitable for advanced modulation formats such as PAM4 and PAM8. The dependence of the Vπ on the modulation frequency was also examined. As shown in Figure 3 (b), Vπ remains stable across a wide frequency range from 1Hz to 1MHz. More detailed results are shown in Figure S5. Similar measurements were performed over a range of on-chip optical powers up to 1.17W, and the results are shown in Figure S6. This flat frequency response contrasts with the pronounced low-frequency instability previously reported for lithium niobate modulators with gold CPWs 31. A small fluctuation (< 0.1V) in Vπ between 1kHz and 100kHz is attributed to dielectric relaxation intrinsic to the Cu–LiTaO3 stack. Such effects arise from slow polarization dynamics or charge trapping in the ferroelectric layer when the modulation frequency approaches the characteristic relaxation rate. The magnitude and frequency of this fluctuation remain unchanged as the on-chip optical power increases from 1mW to 1.17W, confirming that is not due to optical intensity-dependent photorefractive effects. As indicated by the stable quasi-static Vπ, the modulator exhibits excellent long-term stability, showing only a 0.4 dB bias drift over 15 hours at 1.75mW on-chip power (Figure 3(c)). This stability removes the need for active thermal biasing and its associated power-hungry heaters 30. More detailed bias-drift measurement results are provided in Figure S7. Figure 3 (d) presents the measured EO response up to 110GHz. The 3 dB EO bandwidth reaches 40GHz for a 16mm-long device and 100GHz for a 6mm-long device, both with a 6µm electrode gap. The simulated EO response is derived from the measured electrical response and agrees well with the experimental data, validating the measurement. Simulations further indicate that the 3-dB EO bandwidth is approximately 10% higher than that of comparable gold-electrode devices (Figure S8). These results demonstrate that the copper-electrode-based modulators combine high EO bandwidth with low drive voltage, enabling high-speed optical communication applications.

Optical Communications. To demonstrate the exceptional performance of our Cu-TFLT MZM, we performed a high-speed intensity-modulation and direct-detection (IMDD) signaling experiment. The experimental apparatus for this task is illustrated in Figure 4(a) and further described in the Methods. We generated and received PAM4 and PAM8 data signals with symbol rates between 144GBd and 208GBd. Figure 4 (b) displays the measured bit error ratios (BER) of the various PAM signals as a function of symbol rate. The horizontal dashed lines indicate the thresholds for typical soft-decision (SD) forward-error correction (FEC) with 25% and 15% overhead, and for hard-decision (HD) FEC with 7% overhead. The results show that we can transmit 180GBd PAM8 signals and 208GBd PAM4 signals while the respective BER of 3.76×10−2 and 3.56×10−2 are still below the 25% SD-FEC limit. In Figure 4 (c), we further calculate the generalized mutual information (GMI) of our measurements based on log-likelihood ratios by using an additive white Gaussian noise channel model 32. The dashed curves depict the achievable information rate (AIR), which is the product of the GMI and the symbol rate. The solid curves in Figure 4 (c) show the net data rates for measurements with BER below the 25% SD-FEC limit, where the net data rates are determined by multiplying the transmitted line rates with the code rate that is associated with the normalized GMI threshold, extracted from 33. The results indicate that the highest AIR of 449Gbit/s is achieved by using PAM8 signals at a symbol rate of 176GBd. This corresponds to a net data rate of 423Gbit/s, which is on par with results demonstrated for high-bandwidth thin-film lithium niobate MZMs 34. Comparison of these data rates and other metrics achieved in this work along with those from other state-of-the-art lithium niobate and lithium tantalate modulators are available in Table S1. It should be noted that some of the results such as the PAM4 symbol rate were limited by the bandwidth of our driver electronics, not by the MZM itself.
paper_content.methods:
Copper Damascene Fabrication Flow. To begin with, the TFLT PICs were cladded with a 2.5µm-thick silicon dioxide layer by plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD). This cladding layer will embed the subsequently formed copper electrodes. The layout for these electrodes was defined with a DUV stepper lithography (ASML PAS 5500/350C) and transferred as preforms into the cladding layer through fluorine-based dry etching in a reactive ion etcher. These preforms were coated with 10nm of titanium (Ti) and 100nm of copper (Cu) through sputtering (Alliance-Concept DP 650). The titanium layer serves as a barrier to prevent copper from diffusing into the surrounding dielectric 41. It also provides adhesion to a subsequently sputtered copper layer acting as a seed to facilitate copper electroplating. The electroplating was performed in a Silicet Electroplating unit and contributed to a 2.8µm thick copper layer with low resistivity (2.04µΩcm). Chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) was employed to remove the excess copper, leaving copper only in the etched preforms with a final thickness of 1.8µm. This relatively thick metal layer minimizes microwave losses in the CPW electrodes across frequencies ranging from tens of GHz to 110GHz (Figure S14). Since the electrodes are embedded within a SiO2 cladding layer and share a common top surface, their thickness can be indirectly monitored by measuring the thickness of nearby SiO2 windows using spectroscopic reflectometry, as shown in Figure 1 (c). Subsequently, a 100nm-thick silicon nitride passivation layer was deposited with PECVD to prevent copper oxidation. The electrode pads were then opened and capped with gold (Au) for efficient and stable electrical probing. Finally, chip singulation was achieved through a combination of dry etching - standard reactive ion etching for LT and silicon dioxide, deep reactive ion etching for silicon - and backside grinding. This process ensures smooth facets for edge coupling to single-mode fibers.

Data Transmission Apparatus. An external-cavity laser (ECL, 17.8dBm at 1550nm) provides the optical carrier. A high-speed arbitrary-waveform generator (AWG, M8199B, Keysight) is used to generate the electrical drive signal, which is fed to the CPW of the MZM via a 20cm-long RF cable, a broadband RF amplifier, and a 110GHz RF probe. We synthesize various pulse-amplitude modulation (PAM) signals based on pseudo-random bit sequences and apply root-raised cosine pulse-shaping filters with a roll-off of β = 0.05. We account for the frequency-dependent RF loss up to the input of the feeding probe by applying a linear minimum-mean-square-error (MMSE) predistortion. The CPW is terminated by a 50Ω resistor via a second 110GHz RF probe. As previously demonstrated in Figure 3 (c), the EO stability of the Cu-TFLT modulator allows reliable DC biasing at the quadrature point for intensity modulation with a bias-T attached to the second probe. The optical power at the output fiber of the MZM operated at the quadrature point is 5.6dBm, which exceeds the power requirements in typical specifications for high-speed optical ethernet transceivers 42. Still, an additional erbium-doped fiber amplifier (EDFA) was needed in the experiment to reach sufficient power levels for the high-speed photodiode (8.5dBm) at the receiver. Note that a practical transceiver implementation could rely on a sufficiently broadband amplifier after the photodiode, thereby rendering the EDFA unnecessary. In our experiments, the out-of-band amplified spontaneous-emission (ASE) noise of the EDFA is suppressed by a tunable bandpass filter (BPF), and a variable optical attenuator (VOA) is used to adjust a power level of 8.5dBm at the input of the photodiode. The electrical signal at the photodiode output is digitized by a real-time oscilloscope (RTO, UXR 1004A, Keysight) with an analogue bandwidth of 105GHz and a sampling rate of 256 GSa/s. The data is finally extracted by offline receiver DSP (Rx-DSP), which contains resampling to 2 Sa/symbol, timing recovery, linear Sato equalization, and an additional decision-directed least-mean-square (DD-LMS) equalizer.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript presents an advancement in the implementation of electro-optic modulator using a copper Damascene process with ~10% lower microwave loss compared to conventional gold electrodes. The demonstration of high data rates (416 and 540 Gbit/s) and compatibility with industry-standard processes are useful for next-generation photonic-electronic co-integration. This work can be considered for publication in Nature Communications after addressing the following issues.
1. The copper Damascene process is well-described, and the use of CMP for planarization is a key technique for hybrid bonding. However, more details on the uniformity and yield of the process across the 4-inch wafer would strengthen the scalability arguement. Statistical data on device performance variation would be beneficial.
2. While comparisons are made with silver-based modulators, a more detailed table comparing key metrics (e.g., VpL, bandwidth, loss, data rate) with recent LN and LT modulators would help contextualize the advancements.
3. The manuscript emphasizes the potential for chip-on-wafer bonding, but no actual bonding or co-integration results are shown. A preliminary demonstration or cross-section image of a bonded structure would greatly strengthen the claim.
4. It would be beneficial if the authors could provide more detailed information on how the electrode structure (e.g., gap width, signal line width, thickness) was specifically designed to achieve phase velocity matching between the microwave and optical modes.
5. While Supplementary Figure S8 shows microwave loss stability over 7 months, more information on environmental stability (e.g., temperature cycling, humidity tests) would be valuable for assessing suitability in commercial applications. This is especially relevant given copper’s susceptibility to oxidation and diffusion.
6. A critical metric for the practical deployment of Mach-Zehnder modulators (MZMs) in communication systems is the long-term stability of the operating bias point. The authors comprehensively demonstrate the remarkable stability of the half-wave voltage across frequency (Fig. 3c, Suppl. Fig. S2). However, they do not present data on the dynamics of the relative output intensity with the bias set to quadrature over extended operating time.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors present a thin-film lithium tantalate (TFLT) modulator utilizing a copper damascene process. I am not able to recommend the manuscript for publication in a high-profile journal such as Nature Communications due to the following major weaknesses:
1. The Damascene process is claimed to be a key innovation of this work, but its practical advantages for optical transmission applications are insufficiently demonstrated, particularly in achieving notably lower propagation loss [Optica 5, 884-892 (2018)].
2. The observed improvement in electro-optic modulation performance stems primarily from the lower electrical resistivity of copper, rather than structural or process-related innovations.
3. The work employs a sophisticated Damascene fabrication technique, but the overall device performance shows only marginal improvement compared with their previous work [Optica 11, 1614-1620 (2024)].
In addition, below are my technical comments/questions:
1. Figure 2b shows that the resistivity of Ag is lower than that of Au and Cu. Should Ag be a better material than Cu for metal electrodes in electro-optic (EO) modulators?
2. Compared with the Ag-electrode-based TFLT EO modulator reported in [Optica 11, 1614-1620 (2024)], the measured bit error ratios (BER) for both PAM8 and PAM4 signals as a function of symbol rate demonstrate only marginal improvement. What are the reasons for this limited performance?
3. How did the authors determine the thickness and geometry of the Cu electrodes to achieve lower microwave loss? How was the thickness controlled precisely through Cu planarization method?
4. In Figure 3c, why does V_π fluctuate between 10^3 and 10^5 Hz?
5. Figure S7 shows that the EO modulation performance depends on the structure of the Cu electrodes. It is crucial to evaluate how the electrode structure impacts optical transmission, as this will consequently influence the overall modulation performance.

in [Optica 5, 884-892 (2018)] involved producing silicon dioxide cladded silicon nitride
waveguides. Specifically, it relies on etching smooth preforms followed by LPCVD
deposition of silicon nitride and planarization of the resulting material stack. This resulted
in the formation of silicon nitride waveguides with ultrasmooth sidewalls which were
instrumental in reducing optical propagation losses in silicon nitride photonic integrated
circuits.
Unlike this Damascene process for silicon nitride photonic waveguides, the process
reported in this work is for copper microwave electrodes. Direct etching of copper is
particularly challenging because copper does not form volatile byproducts, making it
difficult to produce clean, well-defined features. Although alternative methods such as lift-
off can avoid direct etching, its resolution becomes limited when the copper layer is thick
(e.g., >0.5 µm) or when the pattern has a high aspect ratio. Lift-off also leaves copper
sidewalls exposed, which complicates the subsequent deposition of diffusion barrier
layers (e.g., Ti, Ta, TaN, etc.) that are essential in modern interconnect technologies to
prevent copper diffusion. In addition, metal deposition for lift-off is typically performed by
evaporation due to its superior directionality compared to other physical vapor deposition
(PVD) methods such as sputtering. However, evaporation is inherently slow (~20 nm/min)
and costly, making it impractical for depositing thick copper films or for large-scale

mentioned in our work, one of the key structural effects contributing to our lower resistivity
electrodes is copper’s self-annealing effect as quantified in Figure 2(c). As discussed in
the Electrical Transmission section of our work, this effect is well studied in the
microelectronics community [J. Appl. Phys. 86, 2516-2525 (1999)]. During this process,
the resistivity of electroplated copper decreases after deposition as a result of grain growth
within its crystallographic structure. Given electroplated copper’s dominance in
microelectronics, studies examining this effect in copper films deposited by other means,
such as by evaporation or sputtering, are a little scarcer. However, early work relying on
thinner evaporated or sputtered copper films seem to rely on an additional annealing step
6
to bring down the resistance of their copper films to bulk values [J. Electrochem. Soc. 139,
992 (1992); Electrochem. Solid-State Lett. 2, 534 (1999); Appl. Phys. Lett. 81, 3774-3776
(2002); Phys. Rev. B 102, 165102 (2020)]. Such effects could relate to our observed lower
microwave losses compared to prior work involving modulators relying on lithium niobate
and evaporated copper [Photonics Res. 10, 2380-2387 (2022)]. Though these
observations do not definitely conclude the relevance of the structural benefits of using
electroplated copper over evaporated copper, they do justify an exhaustive comparison of
the effects of both types of copper on electro-optic modulation, which we believe would
be more appropriate for a more specialized study.
Furthermore, as emphasized in our reply to the reviewer’s previous comment, the
structural benefits that come with the Damascene process provide additional advantages
beyond modest propagation-loss reduction: (i) CMP planarization that enables chip-on-
wafer hybrid bonding, and (ii) compatibility with multilayer metallization flows well-
established in commercial microfabrication. These two factors greatly contribute to the
industrial scalability of our platform. We have clarified this point in the revised Discussion
and supported it with AFM planarity data (new Supplementary Figure S13).
3. The work employs a sophisticated Damascene fabrication technique, but the overall
device performance shows only marginal improvement compared with their previous work
[Optica 11, 1614-1620 (2024)].
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment. While the overall communication
performance shows only modest improvement compared with our previous Ag-electrode-
based TFLT modulator, the main contribution of this work lies in establishing a scalable
and standardized copper Damascene process for Pockels modulators.
From a device perspective, the achievable data rate and BER depend on both microwave
and optical factors. The microwave and microwave–optical performance of our Cu-based
device are comparable to those of the Ag-based modulator, as expected from the similar
resistivity of the two metals. However, our device offers improved optical characteristics,
including lower coupling and transmission losses and higher extinction ratio, which
together enable slightly better transmission performance.
The limited BER improvement is therefore not a reflection of material or design limitations,
but rather of the fact that the Ag and Cu devices are already near the performance ceiling
defined by the experimental setup. The key advance of the present work is the
demonstration of a scalable, low-loss, and planarized copper platform that preserves
the high-speed capability of TFLT modulators while enabling large-scale electronic–
photonic co-integration, which is an essential step toward practical and manufacturable
high-bandwidth EO systems.
1. Figure 2b shows that the resistivity of Ag is lower than that of Au and Cu. Should Ag be
a better material than Cu for metal electrodes in electrooptic (EO) modulators?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s comment. While silver has the lowest bulk
resistivity among elemental metals used in microelectronics (1.59 μΩ·cm vs. 1.68 μΩ·cm
for copper, only 5.6% higher), this small difference becomes negligible in thin films, where
resistivity is dominated by fabrication conditions. In practice, thin-film silver does not
necessarily outperform copper and suffers from diffusion and sulfidation issues that are
difficult to control. In addition, electroplating and CMP processes are not well optimized
for silver. In contrast, the copper Damascene process we use is mature, cost-effective,
and widely adopted in microelectronics and silicon photonics. It provides planarized
surfaces, multilayer routing, and direct compatibility with chip-on-wafer bonding - key for
minimizing parasitic and enabling dense 3D integration. Such manufacturing maturity and
integration capabilities are generally lacking in silver-based processes. Therefore, we
respectively don’t think silver is a better material for scalable and reliable applications of
EO modulators. We have added the following passages in the main text to clarify these
points.
For context, Figure 2(b) presents the bulk resistivity of the seven most conductive
elemental metals commonly used in microelectronics and photonics. Although thin
films are typically employed in these applications, their resistivity depends on
thickness and fabrication process; thus, bulk values are used here for a general
comparison. Silver (1.59 μΩ·cm) exhibits the lowest resistivity, followed by copper
(1.59 μΩ·cm), which is only 5.6% higher, and gold (2.21 μΩ·cm) which is 39%
higher. We focus on copper and gold due to the impracticality of using silver (see
Discussion).
From a materials perspective, metals with lower resistivity reduce microwave loss.
Gold electrodes are conventionally used in bulk lithium niobate modulators due to
their relatively low resistivity, chemical stability, and ease of fabrication by
evaporation and lift-off or electroplating followed by etching. With the emergence
of thin-film platforms and growing demands for high-speed data connectivity,
replacing conventional gold electrodes with copper Damascene electrodes has
become strategically important. Copper offers lower resistivity, improved voltage-
bandwidth performance, and compatibility with scalable electronic integration.
Although silver has slightly lower resistivity than copper, it suffers from diffusion
and sulfidation issues that cannot be effectively addressed as copper. Moreover,
silver's electroplating and CMP processes are less mature. Consequently, despite
its marginal electrical advantage, silver is less reliable and less cost-effective for
large-scale integration. on.
8
2. Compared with the Ag-electrode-based TFLT EO modulator reported in [Optica 11,
1614-1620 (2024)], the measured bit error ratios (BER) for both PAM8 and PAM4 signals
as a function of symbol rate demonstrate only marginal improvement. What are the
reasons for this limited performance?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment. The achievable data rate and
corresponding BER are influenced by (i) microwave properties such as impedance
matching and propagation loss, (ii) microwave–optical interactions such as phase-velocity
matching, and (iii) purely optical factors including coupling loss, on-chip transmission loss,
and extinction ratio. In terms of the microwave and microwave-optical performance, our
Cu-electrode-based modulators are similar to those of the Ag-electrode-based TFLT
devices. However, our device demonstrates distinct optical advantages - namely, a fiber-
to-chip coupling loss as low as 3 dB per facet, on-chip transmission loss of only 1 dB, and
an extinction ratio exceeding 20 dB (Supplementary Figure S1). These improvements
contribute to the slightly higher data transmission rates we observe relative to the Ag-
electrode-based counterpart.
While the improvement in data rate is modest, we emphasize that the achieved high
symbol rates primarily validate the intrinsic high-speed capability of our modulator, which
arises from the Pockels effect and the optimized co-design of the traveling-wave
electrodes and optical waveguides. High data rates alone, however, do not directly
translate to energy-efficient operation. As discussed in [OFC 2025, M3C.1], the ultimate
goal of reducing drive voltage and increasing bandwidth is to minimize RF attenuation and
energy consumption. Nonetheless, all the hard work in achieving the above two goals can
be wiped off if the device suffers from high optical insertion loss, as the resulting low optical
output power undermines overall system efficiency.
Of course, a comprehensive assessment of energy efficiency in EO modulators must
consider not only the intrinsic device performance but also the energy consumption of
broadband RF amplifiers and digital signal processing (DSP) modules required for signal
recovery [Nat. Electron. 6, 910–921 (2023)]. Such an analysis lies beyond the scope of
the present study, whose primary objective is to demonstrate the integration of the Cu
Damascene process with Pockels-based platforms (lithium tantalate and lithium niobate).
This approach preserves the intrinsic advantages of these materials (i.e., low loss and
high-speed modulation), while paving the way for large-scale electronic–photonic co-
integration.
Lastly, it is important to note that the measured data transmission rate is also limited by
the bandwidth of the RF components used in the experimental setup rather than the
modulator itself. As shown in [IEEE Photon. Technol. Lett. 35, 850–853 (2023)], the
achievable modulation rate scales with the available RF bandwidth. With the ongoing
development of higher-bandwidth RF electronics, the Cu-TFLT modulators introduced
9
here are expected to support substantially higher data rates, as discussed in [J. Lightwave
Technol. 41, 3674–3679 (2023)] and [OFC 2025, Th4B.7].
3. How did the authors determine the thickness and geometry of the Cu electrodes to
achieve lower microwave loss? How was the thickness controlled precisely through Cu
planarization method?
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point concerning the
methodology behind our modulator design. As described in Supplementary Information
Section II, we used Ansys Q2D to model the microwave transmission properties of the
electrodes. This includes microwave losses. To determine the thickness that achieves
lower losses, we performed simulations of CPW electrodes with varying metal thicknesses.
The results show that microwave losses approach an asymptotic minimum beyond a
certain thickness. For example, at 20 GHz, the metal thickness should exceed 1.6 µm to
achieve low loss; at 40 GHz, this requirement decreases to 1.2 µm, and at frequencies up
to 100 GHz, a thickness greater than 0.6 µm is sufficient. This trend arises from the skin
effect in metals. We have included these simulation results in new Supplementary Figure
S14.
It is worth noting that our copper Damascene process readily supports the fabrication of
electrodes several micrometers thick. The maximum thickness is mainly limited by the
ability to uniformly coat the trench sidewalls with the diffusion barrier and copper seed
layers during sputtering. This capability not only ensures a “safe” electrode thickness for
achieving low microwave loss, but also enables the realization of deep vias for signal
routing, which is crucial for the seamless integration of driving circuits with photonic
integrated circuits [IEEE J. Sel. Top. Quantum Electron. 25, 1 (2019)].
Since the electrodes are fully embedded within the oxide cladding and share a common
top surface, their thickness can be monitored by measuring the oxide window thickness
via spectroscopic reflectometry, as illustrated in main text Figure 1(c).
We have added the following passage in the main text Methods to address these points:
This relatively thick metal layer minimizes microwave losses of the CPW electrodes
across frequencies ranging from tens of GHz to 110 GHz (Supplementary
Information). Since the electrodes are embedded within a SiO cladding layer and
2
share a common top surface, their thickness can be indirectly monitored by
measuring the thickness of nearby SiO windows using spectroscopic reflectometry,
2
as shown in Figure 1(c).
4. In Figure 3c, why does V_π fluctuate between 10^3 and 10^5 Hz?
Pockels modulator, the Vπ should remain constant across frequency, as the electro-optic
effect is inherently linear and instantaneous. In practice, however, real materials and
electrode properties introduce secondary effects that lead to frequency-dependent
variations. At high modulation frequencies (e.g., in the tens of gigahertz range), the
propagating electrical signal experiences attenuation due to factors such as skin effect
and dielectric losses along the traveling-wave electrodes. This attenuation reduces the
effective voltage applied to the modulation region, resulting in an apparent increase in Vπ.
At lower frequencies (e.g., below 1 MHz, as explored in this work), slow polarization
dynamics, charge trapping, or ionic relaxation within the ferroelectric lithium tantalate can
induce small variations in the effective refractive index. These slow processes are unable
to follow high-frequency modulation and therefore only manifest when the modulation
frequency approaches or falls below their characteristic relaxation frequencies. The mild
fluctuation of Vπ (<0.1 V) observed between 10^3 Hz and 10^5 Hz can thus be attributed
to such dielectric relaxation effects intrinsic to the Cu–LiTaO stack. Similar low-frequency
3
anomalies have been reported in thin-film lithium niobate modulators, where slow
polarization and interface charging give rise to enhanced or oscillatory electro-optic
response in the 1 kHz to 100 kHz range [Holzgrafe et al., Opt. Express 32, 3619 (2024)].
Interestingly, the magnitude and position of the observed fluctuation do not change when
the on-chip optical power is increased from 1 mW to 1.17 W (Supplementary Figure S3,
indicating that it is not caused by photorefractive effects, but rather by intrinsic dielectric
relaxation.
However, we agree with the reviewer on the importance of acknowledging its presence
and pointing to its potential origin. To address this point, we added the following passage
in the Electro-optic Modulation section in the main text:
A small fluctuation (< 0.1 V) in Vpi between 1 kHz and 100 kHz is attributed to
dielectric relaxation intrinsic to the Cu–LiTaO stack. Such effects arise from slow
3
polarization dynamics or charge trapping in the ferroelectric layer when the
modulation frequency approaches the characteristic relaxation rate. The magnitude
and frequency of this fluctuation remain unchanged as the on-chip optical power
increases from 1 mW to 1.17 W, confirming that it is not due to photorefractive
effects.
5. Figure S7 shows that the EO modulation performance depends on the structure of the
Cu electrodes. It is crucial to evaluate how the electrode structure impacts optical
transmission, as this will consequently influence the overall modulation performance.
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising the potential issue of the copper electrode’s
structure affecting the optical transmission of the modulator. The slow-wave (capacitively
loaded) CPW electrodes used here are well-established designs that have been
11
experimentally demonstrated in prior works [IEEE Trans. Microw. Theory Techn., 42, 1918
(1994); Optica 8, 357 (2021); APL Photonics 7, 020802 (2022)]. These microstructured
“T-rail” geometries reduce current crowding near the electrode gaps, thereby lowering
microwave loss, while maintaining a similar electric field distribution across the optical
waveguide to preserve modulation efficiency.
As a result, the optical transmission loss remains primarily governed by the electrode gap,
as in the case of conventional CPW electrodes. The impact of the electrode gap on optical
transmission loss has been depicted in main text Figure 3(a). The slow-wave geometry
itself does not introduce additional optical absorption or scattering beyond this
dependence.
Our implementation of the slow-wave structures in new Supplementary Figure S12
primarily serves as a proof of concept to validate the Cu Damascene process for defining
fine “T-rail” features with high fidelity and thus electrode with low-loss. As shown in new
Supplementary Figure S13(a), the process faithfully reproduces these structures with
excellent edge definition, confirming that the Damascene platform can support future
iterations employing optimized slow-wave electrodes for further bandwidth and loss
improvements.
12

The authors argue that “unlike the Damascene process for silicon nitride photonic waveguides, the process reported here is for copper microwave electrodes.” However, the ultimate goal of any process innovation should be to enhance device performance. Both the academic and industrial communities favor processes that are sustainable, simpler, more efficient, and more reliable. In this connection, compared with the same group’s earlier work using Ag electrodes [Optica 11, 1614 1620 (2024)], the considerably more complicated “copper Damascene process” introduced here yields only mild improvement in performance. This substantially diminishes the claimed advantage of a copper based platform relying on Damascene processing. Therefore, only if this complicated process delivers a substantial performance enhancement would I be able to support its publication.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The conversion between electrical and optical signals underpins modern optical communication systems and increasingly requires tight co-integration with electronics at short length scales. Thin-film lithium tantalate has emerged as a promising electro-optic platform due to its large Pockels coefficient, low bias drift, and high power handling, yet its integration with standardized microelectronic processes remains limited. Here we show that incorporating the copper Damascene process into thin-film lithium tantalate modulators enables a scalable, electronics-compatible fabrication approach. The resulting devices exhibit approximately 10% lower microwave loss than conventional gold-electrode designs, while simultaneously supporting watt-level on-chip optical power handling and maintaining a stable quasi-static half-wave voltage from 1 Hz to 1 MHz, with a bias point drift of only 0.4 dB over a 15-hour period when operated at 1.75 mW on-chip optical power. High-speed transmission experiments demonstrate line rates of 416 Gbit/s (PAM4) and 540 Gbit/s (PAM8) below the 25% soft-decision forward-error-correction threshold, together with watt-level on-chip optical power handling. These results establish a practical route toward scalable chip-on-wafer integration of electro-optic modulators with microelectronic circuits.

---

## Introduction

Integrated electro-optic (EO) modulators provide a scalable platform for converting information between electrical and optical domains, serving as key building blocks for high-capacity optical communications 1–3 and emerging chip-to-chip interconnects 4,5. Recent progress in thin-film lithium niobate and thin-film lithium tantalate photonics has transformed traditional bulk devices 6,7. The adoption of a layered “on-insulator” structure, combined with improved etching techniques, enables strong optical confinement and allows electrodes to be placed closer to the waveguide, thereby enhancing modulation efficiency. This structure also facilitates velocity matching between optical and microwave signals, resulting in higher modulation bandwidths. However, as the electrode gap is reduced to achieve tighter optical confinement and stronger modulation, the currents in the signal line and ground plane become increasingly concentrated near the gap due to the electromagnetic proximity effect 8. This enhanced current concentration increases the per-unit-length resistance of the transmission line, leading to higher microwave loss. The resulting loss limits further improvements in voltage–bandwidth performance. Employing electrodes with periodic microstructured “T-rails” mitigates the proximity effect by introducing a larger effective gap while preserving the electric-field distribution required for efficient modulation 9–12. An alternative approach to reducing microwave loss replaces conventional gold electrodes with low-resistivity metals, such as copper which has a resistivity approximately 24% lower than gold 13.

While continuous efforts have been made to extend the voltage–bandwidth performance of thin-film lithium niobate and lithium tantalate modulators 14,15, most reported devices remain standalone prototypes, requiring bulky electrical probes and external control electronics. Meanwhile, AI-based applications are driving an ever-growing demand for higher data throughput, lower latency, and improved energy efficiency in modern computing systems 16. To meet these requirements, co-packaged optics (CPO) has emerged as a transformative technology that tightly integrates photonics and electronics 17. Such integration reduces high-frequency signal degradation, reduces energy consumption, and enables large-scale system scalability. Among various integration approaches, three-dimensional (3D) integration, as illustrated in Figure 1(a), offers the shortest metal interconnects by vertically stacking photonic and electronic chips, thereby minimizing signal loss and improving overall efficiency 18. While this stacking is typically achieved through flip-chip bonding using microbumps 19, the industry is transitioning toward hybrid copper-copper bonding 20. In this approach, copper surfaces are directly joined through thermally activated diffusion, eliminating solder interfaces and thereby reducing parasitic effects. A key enabler of this transition is planarized copper metallization achieved via the copper Damascene process, already widely adopted in both microelectronics 21 and silicon photonics 22. However, ferroelectric photonic platforms still rely on conventional gold electrodes, highlighting the need for further innovation to achieve fully integrated, high-performance photonic–electronics systems.

Here, we address this challenge by incorporating the copper Damascene process into the fabrication of lithium tantalate photonic integrated circuits (PICs). This approach leverages a mature, low-cost, and widely adopted method used for metallization in microelectronics and silicon photonics. Using this process, we demonstrate integrated electro-optic modulators with microwave losses approximately 10% lower than those employing conventional gold electrodes, while preserving the intrinsic benefits of thin-film lithium tantalate, including low optical loss, high modulation efficiency, and broad modulation bandwidth. The resulting planar electrode surface also supports direct chip-on-chip and chip-on-wafer bonding with driver electronics.

---

## Results

Fabrication. The devices were fabricated from a commercially available X-cut thin-film lithium tantalate (TFLT) wafer (NANOLN), which consists of 600nm of lithium tantalate (LiTaO3, LT), 4.7µm of SiO2, and a 525µm-thick high-resistivity silicon substrate. The TFLT PICs were manufactured using an etching technique based on a diamond-like carbon hard mask, which can reliably produce both lithium niobate and lithium tantalate PICs 23,24. The etch depth of the LT was 320nm, leaving a 280nm-thick slab for efficient electro-optic modulation and proper phase matching between microwave and optical signals.

Next, the copper Damascene process, outlined in Figure 1(b), was introduced to fabricate traveling-wave electrodes. This Damascene process differs from silicon nitride Damascene methods 25, which reduce optical propagation losses in waveguides whereas we apply it to copper electrodes to minimize microwave loss. In this process, dielectric trenches are patterned and filled by electroplated copper followed by chemical–mechanical polishing (CMP). This process produces well-defined electrodes with a smooth surface potentially suitable for chip-on-wafer bonding. Further information on the fabrication is available in the Methods. Figure 1 (c) shows two fabricated Cu-TFLT MZMs extending over an effective modulation length of 6mm. Figure 1 (d) illustrates the fabricated 4-inch wafer with hundreds of Cu-TFLT MZMs, highlighting its potential for scalable integration of next-generation photonic systems. To improve the wafer’s uniformity following the CMP process, inactive regions feature a filler copper pattern, which is visible in Figure 1(c-e). As respectively shown in Figure 1(e-g), each modulator consists of 50:50 1×2 multimode interference (MMI) couplers, EO phase shifters operating in a push-pull configuration, and double-layer tapers for enhanced PIC-to-fiber coupling efficiency 26 (Figure S1). As illustrated in Figure 1(f), the tight confinement of the modulator’s microwave and optical modes ensures strong overlap between the two fields and thus enhanced modulation efficiency.

Electrical Transmission. To assess the potential of copper as an electrode material for high-performance modulators, we characterized the electrical properties of fabricated copper Damascene CPWs, including resistivity and microwave performance, and compared them with their conventional gold-based counterparts. Figure 2 (a) shows a photograph of the test structures. For context, Figure 2 (b) presents the bulk resistivity of the seven most conductive elemental metals commonly used in microelectronics and photonics. Although thin films are typically employed in these applications, their resistivity depends on thickness and fabrication process; thus, bulk values are used here for a general comparison. Silver (1.59µΩcm) exhibits the lowest resistivity, followed by copper (1.68µΩcm), which is only 5.6% higher, and gold (2.21µΩcm), which is 39% higher 27. We focus on copper and gold due to the impracticality of using silver (see Discussion).

Figure 2 (c) compares the measured resistivity of thin-film gold and copper and its evolution with time. The gold thin film (796nm) was deposited by electron beam evaporation, and the copper thin film (1170nm) by electroplating. Both were formed on silicon carrier wafers with a 2µm silicon dioxide layer and characterized using a four-point probing and mechanical profilometry. The electroplated copper exhibited a 24% decrease in resistivity within 48 hours at room temperature due to self-annealing 28, stabilizing at 2.04µΩcm - approximately 20% lower than that of gold. Studies suggest that the resistivity of electroplated copper could be further reduced to 1.77µΩcm 29 via process optimization. Using these measured values, we modeled the microwave behavior of the fabricated CPWs through full-wave electromagnetic simulations (Figure S2). Figure 2 (d) shows the simulated microwave loss of a 16mm-long copper Damascene CPW with a 6µm gap and a 27µm signal line, alongside simulated CPWs with varying resistivities but identical geometries. The measured microwave loss agrees well with the simulation, validating the model. The data indicate that copper electrodes yield approximately 10% lower microwave loss than gold, while the propagation index and characteristic impedance change by less than 0.3%. The dependence of the microwave effective index on design parameters is provided in Figure S3.

Electro-optic Modulation. A direct approach to assess the modulators’ performance is to measure their EO response, including the quasi-static half-wave voltage (Vπ) and the 3 dB EO bandwidth. Finite-element simulations (COMSOL Multiphysics) were performed to analyze the VπL product and optical loss for various modulator geometries. A design with 6µm electrode gap and a 4µm-wide waveguide was selected. This relatively wide waveguide maintains a similar VπL and optical loss while allowing a larger electrode gap that reduces microwave loss (Figure S4) 30. A 100µm-long adiabatic linear taper connects the modulation region to the single-mode routing waveguide, ensuring single-mode operation. The quasi-static Vπ was measured by applying a low-frequency triangular voltage signal to the CPW electrode and recording the optical output simultaneously. Figure 3 (a) shows the normalized transmission of a modulator as a function of the applied voltage, linearly swept at 100Hz, exhibiting a near-sinusoidal response with a Vπ of 1.7V. For a device length of 16mm, this corresponds to a VπL of 2.7V·cm, closely matching the simulated value of 2.64V·cm. The inset dB-scale plot shows an extinction ratio of 20dB, suitable for advanced modulation formats such as PAM4 and PAM8. The dependence of the Vπ on the modulation frequency was also examined. As shown in Figure 3 (b), Vπ remains stable across a wide frequency range from 1Hz to 1MHz. More detailed results are shown in Figure S5. Similar measurements were performed over a range of on-chip optical powers up to 1.17W, and the results are shown in Figure S6. This flat frequency response contrasts with the pronounced low-frequency instability previously reported for lithium niobate modulators with gold CPWs 31. A small fluctuation (< 0.1V) in Vπ between 1kHz and 100kHz is attributed to dielectric relaxation intrinsic to the Cu–LiTaO3 stack. Such effects arise from slow polarization dynamics or charge trapping in the ferroelectric layer when the modulation frequency approaches the characteristic relaxation rate. The magnitude and frequency of this fluctuation remain unchanged as the on-chip optical power increases from 1mW to 1.17W, confirming that is not due to optical intensity-dependent photorefractive effects. As indicated by the stable quasi-static Vπ, the modulator exhibits excellent long-term stability, showing only a 0.4 dB bias drift over 15 hours at 1.75mW on-chip power (Figure 3(c)). This stability removes the need for active thermal biasing and its associated power-hungry heaters 30. More detailed bias-drift measurement results are provided in Figure S7. This structure also facilitates velocity matching between optical and microwave signals, resulting in higher modulation bandwidths. However, as the electrode gap is reduced to achieve tighter optical confinement and stronger modulation, the currents in the signal line and ground plane become increasingly concentrated near the gap due to the electromagnetic proximity effect 8. ## Paper

## Abstract

The conversion between electrical and optical signals underpins modern optical communication systems and increasingly requires tight co-integration with electronics at short length scales. Thin-film lithium tantalate has emerged as a promising electro-optic platform due to its large Pockels coefficient, low bias drift, and high power handling, yet its integration with standardized microelectronic processes remains limited. Here we show that incorporating the copper Damascene process into thin-film lithium tantalate modulators enables a scalable, electronics-compatible fabrication approach. The resulting devices exhibit approximately 10% lower microwave loss than conventional gold-electrode designs, while simultaneously supporting watt-level on-chip optical power handling and maintaining a stable quasi-static half-wave voltage from 1 Hz to 1 MHz, with a bias point drift of only 0.4 dB over a 15-hour period when operated at 1.75 mW on-chip optical power. High-speed transmission experiments demonstrate line rates of 416 Gbit/s (PAM4) and 540 Gbit/s (PAM8) below the 25% soft-decision forward-error-correction threshold, together with watt-level on-chip optical power handling. These results establish a practical route toward scalable chip-on-wafer integration of electro-optic modulators with microelectronic circuits.

---

## Introduction

Integrated electro-optic (EO) modulators provide a scalable platform for converting information between electrical and optical domains, serving as key building blocks for high-capacity optical communications 1–3 and emerging chip-to-chip interconnects 4,5. Recent progress in thin-film lithium niobate and thin-film lithium tantalate photonics has transformed traditional bulk devices 6,7. The adoption of a layered “on-insulator” structure, combined with improved etching techniques, enables strong optical confinement and allows electrodes to be placed closer to the waveguide, thereby enhancing modulation efficiency. This structure also facilitates velocity matching between optical and microwave signals, resulting in higher modulation bandwidths. However, as the electrode gap is reduced to achieve tighter optical confinement and stronger modulation, the currents in the signal line and ground plane become increasingly concentrated near the gap due to the electromagnetic proximity effect 8. This enhanced current concentration increases the per-unit-length resistance of the transmission line, leading to higher microwave loss. The resulting loss limits further improvements in voltage–bandwidth performance. Employing electrodes with periodic microstructured “T-rails” mitigates the proximity effect by introducing a larger effective gap while preserving the electric-field distribution required for efficient modulation 9–12. An alternative approach to reducing microwave loss replaces conventional gold electrodes with low-resistivity metals, such as copper which has a resistivity approximately 24% lower than gold 13.

While continuous efforts have been made to extend the voltage–bandwidth performance of thin-film lithium niobate and lithium tantalate modulators 14,15, most reported devices remain standalone prototypes, requiring bulky electrical probes and external control electronics. Meanwhile, AI-based applications are driving an ever-growing demand for higher data throughput, lower latency, and improved energy efficiency in modern computing systems 16. To meet these requirements, co-packaged optics (CPO) has emerged as a transformative technology that tightly integrates photonics and electronics 17. Such integration reduces high-frequency signal degradation, reduces energy consumption, and enables large-scale system scalability. Among various integration approaches, three-dimensional (3D) integration, as illustrated in Figure 1(a), offers the shortest metal interconnects by vertically stacking photonic and electronic chips, thereby minimizing signal loss and improving overall efficiency 18. While this stacking is typically achieved through flip-chip bonding using microbumps 19, the industry is transitioning toward hybrid copper-copper bonding 20. In this approach, copper surfaces are directly joined through thermally activated diffusion, eliminating solder interfaces and thereby reducing parasitic effects. A key enabler of this transition is planarized copper metallization achieved via the copper Damascene process, already widely adopted in both microelectronics 21 and silicon photonics 22. However, ferroelectric photonic platforms still rely on conventional gold electrodes, highlighting the need for further innovation to achieve fully integrated, high-performance photonic–electronics systems.

Here, we address this challenge by incorporating the copper Damascene process into the fabrication of lithium tantalate photonic integrated circuits (PICs). This approach leverages a mature, low-cost, and widely adopted method used for metallization in microelectronics and silicon photonics. Using this process, we demonstrate integrated electro-optic modulators with microwave losses approximately 10% lower than those employing conventional gold electrodes, while preserving the intrinsic benefits of thin-film lithium tantalate, including low optical loss, high modulation efficiency, and broad modulation bandwidth. The resulting planar electrode surface also supports direct chip-on-chip and chip-on-wafer bonding with driver electronics.

---

## Results

Fabrication. The devices were fabricated from a commercially available X-cut thin-film lithium tantalate (TFLT) wafer (NANOLN), which consists of 600nm of lithium tantalate (LiTaO3, LT), 4.7µm of SiO2, and a 525µm-thick high-resistivity silicon substrate. The TFLT PICs were manufactured using an etching technique based on a diamond-like carbon hard mask, which can reliably produce both lithium niobate and lithium tantalate PICs 23,24. The etch depth of the LT was 320nm, leaving a 280nm-thick slab for efficient electro-optic modulation and proper phase matching between microwave and optical signals.

Next, the copper Damascene process, outlined in Figure 1(b), was introduced to fabricate traveling-wave electrodes. This Damascene process differs from silicon nitride Damascene methods 25, which reduce optical propagation losses in waveguides whereas we apply it to copper electrodes to minimize microwave loss. In this process, dielectric trenches are patterned and filled by electroplated copper followed by chemical–mechanical polishing (CMP). This process produces well-defined electrodes with a smooth surface potentially suitable for chip-on-wafer bonding. Further information on the fabrication is available in the Methods. Figure 1 (c) shows two fabricated Cu-TFLT MZMs extending over an effective modulation length of 6mm. Figure 1 (d) illustrates the fabricated 4-inch wafer with hundreds of Cu-TFLT MZMs, highlighting its potential for scalable integration of next-generation photonic systems. To improve the wafer’s uniformity following the CMP process, inactive regions feature a filler copper pattern, which is visible in Figure 1(c-e). As respectively shown in Figure 1(e-g), each modulator consists of 50:50 1×2 multimode interference (MMI) couplers, EO phase shifters operating in a push-pull configuration, and double-layer tapers for enhanced PIC-to-fiber coupling efficiency 26 (Figure S1). As illustrated in Figure 1(f), the tight confinement of the modulator’s microwave and optical modes ensures strong overlap between the two fields and thus enhanced modulation efficiency.

Electrical Transmission. To assess the potential of copper as an electrode material for high-performance modulators, we characterized the electrical properties of fabricated copper Damascene CPWs, including resistivity and microwave performance, and compared them with their conventional gold-based counterparts. Figure 2 (a) shows a photograph of the test structures. For context, Figure 2 (b) presents the bulk resistivity of the seven most conductive elemental metals commonly used in microelectronics and photonics. Although thin films are typically employed in these applications, their resistivity depends on thickness and fabrication process; thus, bulk values are used here for a general comparison. Silver (1.59µΩcm) exhibits the lowest resistivity, followed by copper (1.68µΩcm), which is only 5.6% higher, and gold (2.21µΩcm), which is 39% higher 27. We focus on copper and gold due to the impracticality of using silver (see Discussion).

Figure 2 (c) compares the measured resistivity of thin-film gold and copper and its evolution with time. The gold thin film (796nm) was deposited by electron beam evaporation, and the copper thin film (1170nm) by electroplating. Both were formed on silicon carrier wafers with a 2µm silicon dioxide layer and characterized using a four-point probing and mechanical profilometry. The electroplated copper exhibited a 24% decrease in resistivity within 48 hours at room temperature due to self-annealing 28, stabilizing at 2.04µΩcm - approximately 20% lower than that of gold. Studies suggest that the resistivity of electroplated copper could be further reduced to 1.77µΩcm 29 via process optimization. Using these measured values, we modeled the microwave behavior of the fabricated CPWs through full-wave electromagnetic simulations (Figure S2). Figure 2 (d) shows the simulated microwave loss of a 16mm-long copper Damascene CPW with a 6µm gap and a 27µm signal line, alongside simulated CPWs with varying resistivities but identical geometries. The measured microwave loss agrees well with the simulation, validating the model. The data indicate that copper electrodes yield approximately 10% lower microwave loss than gold, while the propagation index and characteristic impedance change by less than 0.3%. The dependence of the microwave effective index on design parameters is provided in Figure S3.

Electro-optic Modulation. A direct approach to assess the modulators’ performance is to measure their EO response, including the quasi-static half-wave voltage (Vπ) and the 3 dB EO bandwidth. Finite-element simulations (COMSOL Multiphysics) were performed to analyze the VπL product and optical loss for various modulator geometries. A design with 6µm electrode gap and a 4µm-wide waveguide was selected. This relatively wide waveguide maintains a similar VπL and optical loss while allowing a larger electrode gap that reduces microwave loss (Figure S4) 30. A 100µm-long adiabatic linear taper connects the modulation region to the single-mode routing waveguide, ensuring single-mode operation. The quasi-static Vπ was measured by applying a low-frequency triangular voltage signal to the CPW electrode and recording the optical output simultaneously. Figure 3 (a) shows the normalized transmission of a modulator as a function of the applied voltage, linearly swept at 100Hz, exhibiting a near-sinusoidal response with a Vπ of 1.7V. For a device length of 16mm, this corresponds to a VπL of 2.7V·cm, closely matching the simulated value of 2.64V·cm. The inset dB-scale plot shows an extinction ratio of 20dB, suitable for advanced modulation formats such as PAM4 and PAM8. The dependence of the Vπ on the modulation frequency was also examined. As shown in Figure 3 (b), Vπ remains stable across a wide frequency range from 1Hz to 1MHz. More detailed results are shown in Figure S5. Similar measurements were performed over a range of on-chip optical powers up to 1.17W, and the results are shown in Figure S6. This flat frequency response contrasts with the pronounced low-frequency instability previously reported for lithium niobate modulators with gold CPWs 31. A small fluctuation (< 0.1V) in Vπ between 1kHz and 100kHz is attributed to dielectric relaxation intrinsic to the Cu–LiTaO3 stack. Such effects arise from slow polarization dynamics or charge trapping in the ferroelectric layer when the modulation frequency approaches the characteristic relaxation rate. The magnitude and frequency of this fluctuation remain unchanged as the on-chip optical power increases from 1mW to 1.17W, confirming that is not due to optical intensity-dependent photorefractive effects. As indicated by the stable quasi-static Vπ, the modulator exhibits excellent long-term stability, showing only a 0.4 dB bias drift over 15 hours at 1.75mW on-chip power (Figure 3(c)). This stability removes the need for active thermal biasing and its associated power-hungry heaters 30. More detailed bias-drift measurement results are provided in Figure S7. The simulated EO response is derived from the measured electrical response and agrees well with the experimental data, validating the measurement. Simulations further indicate that the 3-dB EO bandwidth is approximately 10% higher than that of comparable gold-electrode devices (Figure S8). These results demonstrate that the copper-electrode-based modulators combine high EO bandwidth with low drive voltage, enabling high-speed optical communication applications.

Optical Communications. To demonstrate the exceptional performance of our Cu-TFLT MZM, we performed a high-speed intensity-modulation and direct-detection (IMDD) signaling experiment. The experimental apparatus for this task is illustrated in Figure 4(a) and further described in the Methods. We generated and received PAM4 and PAM8 data signals with symbol rates between 144GBd and 208GBd. Figure 4 (b) displays the measured bit error ratios (BER) of the various PAM signals as a function of symbol rate. The horizontal dashed lines indicate the thresholds for typical soft-decision (SD) forward-error correction (FEC) with 25% and 15% overhead, and for hard-decision (HD) FEC with 7% overhead. The results show that we can transmit 180GBd PAM8 signals and 208GBd PAM4 signals while the respective BER of 3.76×10−2 and 3.56×10−2 are still below the 25% SD-FEC limit. The dashed curves depict the achievable information rate (AIR), which is the product of the GMI and the symbol rate. The solid curves in Figure 4 (c) show the net data rates for measurements with BER below the 25% SD-FEC limit, where the net data rates are determined by multiplying the transmitted line rates with the code rate that is associated with the normalized GMI threshold, extracted from 33. The results indicate that the highest AIR of 449Gbit/s is achieved by using PAM8 signals at a symbol rate of 176GBd. Comparison of these data rates and other metrics achieved in this work along with those from other state-of-the-art lithium niobate and lithium tantalate modulators are available in Table S1. ## Methods

Copper Damascene Fabrication Flow. To begin with, the TFLT PICs were cladded with a 2.5µm-thick silicon dioxide layer by plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD). This cladding layer will embed the subsequently formed copper electrodes. The layout for these electrodes was defined with a DUV stepper lithography (ASML PAS 5500/350C) and transferred as preforms into the cladding layer through fluorine-based dry etching in a reactive ion etcher. These preforms were coated with 10nm of titanium (Ti) and 100nm of copper (Cu) through sputtering (Alliance-Concept DP 650). The titanium layer serves as a barrier to prevent copper from diffusing into the surrounding dielectric 41. It also provides adhesion to a subsequently sputtered copper layer acting as a seed to facilitate copper electroplating. The electroplating was performed in a Silicet Electroplating unit and contributed to a 2.8µm thick copper layer with low resistivity (2.04µΩcm). Chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) was employed to remove the excess copper, leaving copper only in the etched preforms with a final thickness of 1.8µm. This relatively thick metal layer minimizes microwave losses in the CPW electrodes across frequencies ranging from tens of GHz to 110GHz (Figure S14). Since the electrodes are embedded within a SiO2 cladding layer and share a common top surface, their thickness can be indirectly monitored by measuring the thickness of nearby SiO2 windows using spectroscopic reflectometry, as shown in Figure 1 (c). Subsequently, a 100nm-thick silicon nitride passivation layer was deposited with PECVD to prevent copper oxidation. The electrode pads were then opened and capped with gold (Au) for efficient and stable electrical probing. Finally, chip singulation was achieved through a combination of dry etching - standard reactive ion etching for LT and silicon dioxide, deep reactive ion etching for silicon - and backside grinding. This process ensures smooth facets for edge coupling to single-mode fibers.

Data Transmission Apparatus. An external-cavity laser (ECL, 17.8dBm at 1550nm) provides the optical carrier. A high-speed arbitrary-waveform generator (AWG, M8199B, Keysight) is used to generate the electrical drive signal, which is fed to the CPW of the MZM via a 20cm-long RF cable, a broadband RF amplifier, and a 110GHz RF probe. We synthesize various pulse-amplitude modulation (PAM) signals based on pseudo-random bit sequences and apply root-raised cosine pulse-shaping filters with a roll-off of β = 0.05. We account for the frequency-dependent RF loss up to the input of the feeding probe by applying a linear minimum-mean-square-error (MMSE) predistortion. The CPW is terminated by a 50Ω resistor via a second 110GHz RF probe. As previously demonstrated in Figure 3 (c), the EO stability of the Cu-TFLT modulator allows reliable DC biasing at the quadrature point for intensity modulation with a bias-T attached to the second probe. The optical power at the output fiber of the MZM operated at the quadrature point is 5.6dBm, which exceeds the power requirements in typical specifications for high-speed optical ethernet transceivers 42. Still, an additional erbium-doped fiber amplifier (EDFA) was needed in the experiment to reach sufficient power levels for the high-speed photodiode (8.5dBm) at the receiver. Note that a practical transceiver implementation could rely on a sufficiently broadband amplifier after the photodiode, thereby rendering the EDFA unnecessary. In our experiments, the out-of-band amplified spontaneous-emission (ASE) noise of the EDFA is suppressed by a tunable bandpass filter (BPF), and a variable optical attenuator (VOA) is used to adjust a power level of 8.5dBm at the input of the photodiode. The electrical signal at the photodiode output is digitized by a real-time oscilloscope (RTO, UXR 1004A, Keysight) with an analogue bandwidth of 105GHz and a sampling rate of 256 GSa/s. The data is finally extracted by offline receiver DSP (Rx-DSP), which contains resampling to 2 Sa/symbol, timing recovery, linear Sato equalization, and an additional decision-directed least-mean-square (DD-LMS) equalizer.

higher. We focus on copper and gold due to the impracticality of using silver (see
Discussion).
From a materials perspective, metals with lower resistivity reduce microwave loss.
Gold electrodes are conventionally used in bulk lithium niobate modulators due to
their relatively low resistivity, chemical stability, and ease of fabrication by
evaporation and lift-off or electroplating followed by etching. With the emergence
of thin-film platforms and growing demands for high-speed data connectivity,
replacing conventional gold electrodes with copper Damascene electrodes has
become strategically important. Copper offers lower resistivity, improved voltage-
bandwidth performance, and compatibility with scalable electronic integration.
Although silver has slightly lower resistivity than copper, it suffers from diffusion
and sulfidation issues that cannot be effectively addressed as copper. Moreover,
silver's electroplating and CMP processes are less mature. Consequently, despite
its marginal electrical advantage, silver is less reliable and less cost-effective for
large-scale integration. on.
